title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing -- July 24, 2026
headline: The benchmark's nightly scan aged five 2025 news events into 2026, and every one was caught before scoring.
summary: Fifteen governments, cities, and companies were reviewed overnight. Fourteen scores held within the benchmark's five-point confirmation range. A proposed lower score for Ecuador follows a Human Rights Watch investigation into torture and drone strikes by security forces. It has not been applied; the country's published score remains 35.9 out of 100. Separately, the benchmark's own nightly scan cited a border war between Thailand and Cambodia that never happened in 2026. The fighting it described took place in July 2025. Four more events in tonight's scan were also a year out of date, and all five were corrected before any score changed. Bangladesh's score sits just 0.2 points below the benchmark's Functional line after the government let anti-disappearance protections lapse. Waymo's score held after a safety fix that did not hold in practice. Ukraine, Iran, Russia, and Kansas City all confirmed under the same rule: a government or company is scored for what it does, not for what is done to it.

pipeline.queueHandling: Ecuador's proposed downgrade, from 35.9 to 25.6, has not been applied; the published score stands at 35.9. Five scanner date errors were caught and corrected before scoring and never entered the queue.

topSignals.title: The Benchmark Caught Its Own Scanner Citing a 2025 Border War as 2026 News
topSignals.whyItMatters: A border war between Thailand and Cambodia was reported as happening this week. It actually happened a year earlier, and the mistake was caught before either country's score moved.
topSignals.description: Thailand's score held near its published 32.8 out of 100, and Cambodia's held near its published 12.5, both in bands the evidence already supported. The nightly scan had flagged both countries over a border war with at least 38 people killed and about 300,000 displaced, sourced to a single undated Wikipedia summary page. Human Rights Watch's own World Report 2026 states that this fighting happened in July 2025, not July 2026, and no news organization reported any Thailand-Cambodia clash inside the July 10 to July 24, 2026 review window. Both countries were instead scored on real evidence from inside that window: four Chinese refugees Thailand is holding under pressure from Beijing, and a Cambodian anti-scam crackdown that Human Rights Watch found investigated fewer than one in five identified compounds.

evidence.quote: Fighting in July 2025 killed and injured civilians, including children, displaced around 300,000 people, and damaged religious and cultural sites.

evidence.claim: Human Rights Watch reported on July 13, 2026, that Thailand was holding four UNHCR-recognized Chinese refugees at Suan Phlu Immigration Detention Center under pressure from Beijing.

topSignals.title: Four More 2025 Stories Were Mistakenly Scanned as 2026 News, and Caught
topSignals.whyItMatters: A retailer's layoff notice, an airline's settlement, and a record war casualty count were all a year out of date in tonight's scan. Catching stale dates before they reach a score is basic hygiene, and it worked.
topSignals.description: Best Buy's score held near its published 62.5 after a second check found the 161-person Best Buy Health layoff notice that had flagged the company was filed in July 2025, not 2026. Delta Air Lines held near its own published 62.5 the same way: the $8.1 million government settlement the scan cited was announced in July 2025. Ukraine's and Russia's scores held after the scan's civilian-casualty count, described as a record month, turned out to be the United Nations' July 2025 figure. The genuine June 2026 figure, published by the UN's human rights monitoring mission on July 14, 2026, is itself the deadliest month since April 2022: 293 people killed and 1,990 injured.

evidence.claim: The 161-person Best Buy Health layoff notice was filed in California on July 11, 2025, not 2026.
Delta Air Lines' $8.1 million False Claims Act settlement over Payroll Support Program compensation caps was announced in July 2025.

The UN's human rights monitoring mission in Ukraine found June 2026 was the deadliest month since April 2022, with 293 civilians killed and 1,990 injured; the scan's cited casualty record was actually the July 2025 figure.
evidence.source: UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine

topSignals.title: A Proposed Score Cut for Ecuador Follows a Torture and Drone-Strike Investigation, but the Score Has Not Changed
topSignals.whyItMatters: Security forces tortured detainees, dropped munitions on family farms, and fired on fishing boats, and no one was prosecuted. A lower score reflecting that has been proposed, but the public score has not moved yet.
topSignals.description: Ecuador's published score remains 35.9 out of 100, in the Developing band. A Human Rights Watch investigation published July 21, 2026, based on 62 interviews, documents Ecuadorian security forces torturing detainees with electric shocks and water, dropping munitions on rural properties during a March 2026 operation in San Martin, and firing on a fishing vessel from an armed drone. Prosecutors brought no charges, because, HRW found, the soldiers involved provided no evidence. Neither the Ecuadorian nor the US government responded to HRW's questions. Ecuador's first individual review, in May 2026, had already flagged the published 35.9 as an unreviewed placeholder and scheduled a 60-day check on exactly this kind of evidence. A review triggered by the new HRW report proposed a lower score of 25.6. Because competitive elections, an active Constitutional Court, and a broadly free press still function, Ecuador remains in the Developing band under the proposed score too, well above Pakistan's 17.2. The proposal has not been applied.

evidence.quote: They tortured me with electricity, with a taser. They poured water on me and then shocked me, and I passed out.
prosecutors did not file charges because soldiers failed to provide any evidence

evidence.claim: On March 27, 2026, UN Special Procedures experts reported credible information about a rapid deterioration of civic space affecting Indigenous peoples and human rights defenders, including arbitrary detentions and terrorism accusations.

topSignals.title: Bangladesh's Rights Protections Are Rolling Back, and Its Score Sits Just Below the Functional Line
topSignals.whyItMatters: Bangladesh let its anti-disappearance rules lapse and proposed a replacement law that would stop its own human rights body from investigating security forces. Its score sits a fraction of a point from the benchmark's highest confirmed band.
topSignals.description: Bangladesh's published score of 39.8 sits just 0.2 points below the boundary of the Functional band. Human Rights Watch reported on July 19, 2026, the first enforced disappearance since the July 2024 uprising: fisherman Miraj Sheikh was seen being detained by Coast Guard officers on April 10, 2026, and his family was told the next day that he had never been there. The elected government allowed the ordinances that had earned Bangladesh a score increase in June 2026 to lapse, and HRW says the replacement bill would bar the National Human Rights Commission from investigating security forces. The assessed score of 35.0 sits 4.8 points below the published figure, just inside the benchmark's five-point confirmation range, so the published score holds with a watch flag for the next review cycle.

evidence.claim: Human Rights Watch documented the first enforced disappearance since the July 2024 uprising: fisherman Miraj Sheikh was seen detained by Coast Guard officers on April 10, 2026, and his family was told the next day he had never been there.

evidence.quote: allowed these ordinances to lapse, proposing instead laws under which the police would continue to investigate enforced disappearances

topSignals.title: Waymo Said It Fixed a Safety Problem, and the Problem Kept Happening
topSignals.whyItMatters: Dozens of self-driving cars stalled in San Francisco days after Waymo said the issue was solved. Regulators have given the company until the end of July 2026 to fix how its cars detect emergency vehicles.
topSignals.description: Waymo's score held near its published 35.9 out of 100. On July 4, 2026, dozens of Waymo vehicles stalled in San Francisco traffic with depleted batteries, and some had to be towed. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration then gave robotaxi operators until the end of July 2026 to fix emergency-responder detection, a deadline that falls after this review's evidence window closes. San Francisco firefighters have filed at least 31 internal reports since April 2025 describing robotaxis obstructing emergency operations. The assessed score of 31.3 sits 4.6 points below the published figure, inside the confirmation range, so the score holds with a watch flag on the NHTSA deadline outcome.

evidence.claim: NHTSA gave robotaxi operators until the end of July 2026 to fix emergency-responder detection after dozens of Waymo vehicles stalled in San Francisco on July 4, 2026.

topSignals.title: Four Confirmations Test the Same Rule: Governments Are Scored for What They Do, Not What Is Done to Them
topSignals.whyItMatters: A city that resisted federal detention policy saw its score rise. Countries attacked by someone else did not see their scores fall for it. Only a government's own conduct moves its score.
topSignals.description: Ukraine's score held at its published 50.0 after a Russian strike on a defense-industry event in the Kyiv region killed ten people and wounded more than 100 on July 24, 2026. Ukraine's own response, opening an investigation into whether officials properly assessed the risk of holding the event, is what the benchmark scored. Russia's score held at the absolute floor of 0.0 because that strike is Russia's own conduct. Iran's score held near the floor at 2.5 after it executed five political prisoners between July 16 and July 22, 2026, roughly one execution a day. Kansas City's score rose slightly, from a published 35.9 to an assessed 36.9, after federal agents detained at least 30 residents during the World Cup, conduct the benchmark attributed to the federal government, not the city. Kansas City's own mayor joined a 38-government amicus brief, and its council passed a five-year moratorium on new non-municipal detention facilities.

evidence.claim: Kansas City Mayor Quinton Lucas joined seven mayors and 38 local governments in a federal amicus brief, and the City Council passed a five-year moratorium on non-municipal detention facilities, after at least 30 residents were detained by federal agents during the World Cup.
Ukraine's Prosecutor General opened an investigation into whether officials properly assessed the risk of holding a defense-industry event that a July 24, 2026 Russian strike killed ten people at.
evidence.source: UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine

methodologyNotes.name: A Self-Check Catches the Benchmark's Own Scan Citing Old News as Current
methodologyNotes.description: Five times this cycle, the benchmark's nightly news scan cited events that had already happened, dated a year late. The clearest case: the scan reported a Thailand-Cambodia border war on July 24, 2026, with at least 38 people killed and about 300,000 displaced. That fighting was real, but it happened in July 2025, and Human Rights Watch's own World Report 2026 says so in its own words. A retailer's layoff notice, an airline's government settlement, and a wartime casualty record were each a year older than the scan believed. A second check inside the benchmark caught every one of these before they could change a score, and each country or company was instead scored on the real evidence sitting inside the correct two-week window. This is the same kind of internal check that corrected Becton Dickinson's arithmetic on July 23: the system finding and fixing its own mistake before it reaches the public score.

methodologyNotes.name: Conduct Is Scored, Not Victimhood
methodologyNotes.description: The benchmark scores what a government or company does, not what happens to it. Tonight, Ukraine's score held steady even though a Russian strike killed ten people at a Kyiv-region event, because that harm was done to Ukraine, not by it. Iran's and Russia's near-bottom scores held for the opposite reason: their own conduct, five executions in a week for Iran and a strike on Ukrainian civilians for Russia, confirmed what was already priced into the floor. Kansas City's score rose slightly because federal agents, not the city, carried out the detentions, while the city's own council voted to limit future cooperation.

methodologyNotes.name: A Proposed Score Was Already Waiting for This Evidence
methodologyNotes.description: Ecuador's first review, in May 2026, flagged its published score as an unreviewed placeholder and scheduled a 60-day check specifically on torture and extrajudicial-killing cases. The Human Rights Watch investigation published July 21, 2026, based on 62 interviews, is exactly the evidence that check was waiting for. The resulting proposal, from 35.9 to 25.6, reflects security forces' own documented conduct rather than a recalibration of the benchmark's standards, and it has not yet been applied.

dailyOpeningQuestion.text: Bangladesh's published score sits 0.2 points below the benchmark's Functional boundary after its Accountability dimension fell on evidence of a lapsed anti-disappearance ordinance. What would the replacement bill's final text need to preserve for the score to hold at its current reading?
dailyOpeningQuestion.tensionFraming: A country half a point from the benchmark's highest confirmed band is simultaneously rolling back the safeguard that earned it the climb.
